To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lysosomal cysteines proteinases are under developmental control in fetal calf muscles.
cathepsin activity and mRNA levels decrease during fetal growth and that the two cathepsin mRNAs decline in parallel.
the expression of cathepsines B and L decreases strongly during fetal development and that the decrease of cathepsine B is associated with a parallel reduction of its mRNA level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the regulation of the expression of the lysosomal proteinases cathepsin L, B, and H in bovine fetal muscle.
the regulation of the expression of the lysosomal cysteines proteinases during the development of skeletal muscle.
the study of the development of skeletal muscle in the bovine fetus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cathepsin L is a key protease in the degradation of muscle proteins during atrophy, whereas the role of cathepsine B in muscle protein breakdown is less clear.
cathepsins are not involved in the normal turnover of muscle proteins.
cathepsin expression is developmentally regulated and that the expression of cathepsing is not related to muscle fiber type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cathepsin expression and the muscle growth are under the control of the same factors.
the decrease of lysosomal cystein proteinase in skeletal muscle during fetal growth is associated with a parallel decrease of their mRNA levels.
cathepsin expression and activity are developmentally controlled in skeletal muscle, and that the decrease of these enzymes is sufficient to account for their low levels in adult muscles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
lysosomal proteinase activities are not only under developmental control but also regulated by muscle activity.
the expression of the two cathepsin transcripts is regulated during fetal muscle development in a similar way, and this regulation occurs at the level of mRNA accumulation.
the decrease in muscle cathepins during fetal development appears to be sufficient to account for their low levels in adult muscles.
